claim: Recombinant murine ChaC1 at submicromolar enzyme concentrations can degrade a 10 mM solution of reduced glutathione within 1 hr in vitro.
source: At submicromolar enzyme concentrations, recombinant ChaC1 was able to degrade a 10 mM solution of reduced glutathione within 1 hr (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating glutathione degradation by purified ChaC1.

claim: ChaC1 enzymatic activity is selective towards reduced glutathione (GSH) over oxidized glutathione (GSSG).
source: The enzymatic activity was selective towards reduced glutathione (GSH) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1B comparing ChaC1 activity on GSH vs GSSG.

claim: Oxidized glutathione (GSSG) cannot serve as a substrate for ChaC1 degradation.
source: The inability of oxidized glutathione (GSSG) to serve as a substrate for degradation correlated with its inability to bind a Chac1-based optical probe whose fluorescent resonance energy transfer (FRET) signal reflects substrate binding (Figure 1C–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by FRET binding assay data showing GSSG does not bind to ChaC1 probe.

claim: The E116Q mutation abolishes all ChaC1 enzymatic activity.
source: An E116Q mutation abolished all enzymatic activity (Figure 1E), as observed previously (Kumar et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1E and citation to previous work.

claim: ER-localized wild-type ChaC1 forms inappropriate disulfide bonds when expressed in the ER.
source: However, unlike cytosolic ChaC1, which migrates at a position expected of the reduced monomer on non-reducing SDS-PAGE (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), ER-localized ChaC1 migrated as a heterogenous collection of species, consistent with inappropriate disulfide bond formation (compare the reducing and non-reducing SDS-PAGE in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by SDS-PAGE data showing heterogeneous migration patterns on non-reducing gels.

claim: None of ChaC1's four cysteines is likely to play an important role in substrate recognition or catalysis.
source: A model of mouse ChaC1, based on the crystal structure of the homologous γ-glutamyl cyclotransferase (PDB 2RBH) (Kumar et al., 2012), suggested that none of its four cysteines is likely to play an important role in substrate recognition or catalysis.
evidence: Based on structural modeling using homologous protein crystal structure.

claim: The cysteine-free ChaC1 (ChaC1CtoS) no longer forms disulfides when introduced into the ER.
source: As expected, conversion of all four cysteines to serines resulted in a protein that no longer formed disulfides when introduced into the ER (Figure 2A, compare lanes 6 and 7 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by SDS-PAGE data comparing wild-type and CtoS mutant.

claim: The cysteine-free enzyme (ChaC1CtoS) purified from E. coli retains its enzymatic activity.
source: Importantly, the cysteine-free enzyme (ChaC1CtoS) purified from E. coli retained its enzymatic activity (Figure 2C) and specificity for reduced glutathione (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by in vitro enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Glutaredoxin (Grx1) dramatically accelerates the interaction of linked roGFP with glutathione both in vivo and in vitro.
source: Glutaredoxin (Grx1) has been shown to dramatically accelerate the interaction of a linked redox-sensitive green fluorescent protein (roGFP) with glutathione, both in vivo and in vitro (Gutscher et al., 2008; Birk et al., 2013) (cartooned Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: Reduced roGFP2 alone is only slowly oxidized by glutathione.
source: We confirmed the reported ability of a linked Grx1 to accelerate the equilibration of roGFP with a glutathione buffer: alone, reduced roGFP2 was only slowly oxidized by glutathione (Figure 3B), but the linked Grx1 markedly accelerated the oxidation of Grx1-roGFP2 (Figure 3, compare the red traces in panels B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3B showing slow oxidation kinetics.

claim: Linked Grx1 markedly accelerates the oxidation of Grx1-roGFP2 by glutathione.
source: We confirmed the reported ability of a linked Grx1 to accelerate the equilibration of roGFP with a glutathione buffer: alone, reduced roGFP2 was only slowly oxidized by glutathione (Figure 3B), but the linked Grx1 markedly accelerated the oxidation of Grx1-roGFP2 (Figure 3, compare the red traces in panels B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: The rate of Grx1-roGFP2 oxidation by glutathione is concentration-dependent with half-saturation (Kmax0.5) attained at approximately 18 µM GSSG.
source: The rate of probe oxidation by glutathione was concentration-dependent, with half-saturation (Kmax0.5) attained at ∼18 µM GSSG (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Oxidized PDI has a minor role in accelerating the oxidation of Grx1-roGFP2.
source: Importantly, the presence of oxidized PDI had a minor role in further accelerating the oxidation of Grx1-roGFP2, but dominated the oxidation kinetics of roGFP2 alone (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing oxidation kinetics in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Oxidized PDI dominates the oxidation kinetics of roGFP2 alone.
source: Importantly, the presence of oxidized PDI had a minor role in further accelerating the oxidation of Grx1-roGFP2, but dominated the oxidation kinetics of roGFP2 alone (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3B showing PDI effect on roGFP2.

claim: The recovery of ER-Grx1-roGFP2 is accelerated compared with ER-roGFP2 alone following a reductive DTT pulse, with a half-time to recovery of 75.3 ± 7.7 s for Grx1-roGFP2 and 167.3 ± 16.8 s for roGFP2.
source: However the recovery of ER-Grx1-roGFP2 was accelerated compared with ER-roGFP2 alone, with a half-time to recovery of 75.3 ± 7.7 s in case of the former and 167.3 ± 16.8 s in case of the latter (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements from live cell imaging experiments.

claim: Lumenal glutathione directly contributes to the kinetics of ER-Grx1-roGFP2 re-oxidation in vivo.
source: This observation is consistent with a direct contribution of lumenal glutathione to the kinetics of ER-Grx1-roGPF2 re-oxidation in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from the differential recovery kinetics of Grx1-roGFP2 vs roGFP2.

claim: Expression of active ER-ChaC1CtoS abolishes the kinetic advantage of ER-Grx1-roGFP2 over ER-roGFP2 following a reductive pulse.
source: Oxidation of ER-roGFP2 was unaffected by the presence of active ChaC1, but the kinetic advantage of ER-Grx1-roGFP2 over the ER-roGFP2 alone was abolished by expression of an active, glutathione-degrading enzyme in the ER lumen (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging data comparing recovery kinetics in Figure 3G,H.

claim: Cytosolic ChaC1 leads to a marked depletion of total cellular glutathione levels.
source: At similar levels of over-expression, cytosolic ChaC1 led to a marked depletion of total cellular glutathione levels, whereas ER-localized ChaC1CtoS had a more modest effect.
evidence: Supported by ensemble glutathione measurements in stable cell lines.

claim: ER-localized ChaC1CtoS has a more modest effect on total cellular glutathione than cytosolic ChaC1.
source: At similar levels of over-expression, cytosolic ChaC1 led to a marked depletion of total cellular glutathione levels, whereas ER-localized ChaC1CtoS had a more modest effect.
evidence: Supported by ensemble glutathione measurements comparing cytosolic and ER-localized ChaC1.

claim: ER-localized ChaC1CtoS markedly enhances glutathione depletion by low concentrations of buthionine-sulfoxide (BSO).
source: However, ER-localized ChaC1CtoS markedly enhanced glutathione depletion by low concentrations of buthionine-sulfoxide (BSO, an inhibitor of the rate limiting step of glutathione biosynthesis, Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by glutathione measurements in cells treated with BSO shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Cytosolic and ER pools of glutathione equilibrate relatively slowly in mammalian cells.
source: They point to relatively slow equilibration of cytosolic and ER pools of glutathione in mammalian cells.
evidence: Inferred from differential effects of cytosolic vs ER-localized ChaC1 on total cellular glutathione.

claim: ER-targeted expression of active ChaC1 causes profound and selective depletion of lumenal glutathione with modest effects on other cellular pools of glutathione.
source: Given that Grx1-roGFP2 reacts with glutathione with a Kmax0.5 in the 10−5 M range (Figure 3D) the effacement of its kinetic advantage over roGFP2 in the DTT washout experiment, indicated a profound and selective depletion of lumenal glutathione by the ER-targeted expression of active ChaC1, with modest effects on other cellular pools of glutathione.
evidence: Inferred from the abolition of Grx1-roGFP2 kinetic advantage and known Kmax0.5 value.

claim: Maturation of the LDL-R in the ER entails significant rearrangement of its 30 disulfide bonds.
source: Maturation of the LDL-R in the ER entails significant rearrangement of its 30 disulfide bonds (Jansens et al., 2002) and involves the reduced form of the PDI family member ERdj5 (Oka et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on LDL-R maturation.

claim: Maturation of the LDL-R involves the reduced form of the PDI family member ERdj5.
source: Maturation of the LDL-R in the ER entails significant rearrangement of its 30 disulfide bonds (Jansens et al., 2002) and involves the reduced form of the PDI family member ERdj5 (Oka et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Conversion of the LDL-R from its ER to post-ER form is unaffected by the presence of either active or inactive form of ER-ChaC1.
source: Conversion of the LDL-R from its ER to post-ER form was unaffected by the presence of either active or inactive form of ER-ChaC1 and proceeded with a half-life of ∼1 hr in presence or absence of an active glutathione-depleting enzyme in the ER (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by pulse-chase labeling data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: LDL-R maturation proceeds with a half-life of approximately 1 hr in presence or absence of an active glutathione-depleting enzyme in the ER.
source: Conversion of the LDL-R from its ER to post-ER form was unaffected by the presence of either active or inactive form of ER-ChaC1 and proceeded with a half-life of ∼1 hr in presence or absence of an active glutathione-depleting enzyme in the ER (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of pulse-chase data in Figure 4A.

claim: Glutathione depletion has no drastic effect on the early oxidative phase of LDL-R maturation.
source: The non-reducing gel revealed identical accelerated mobility of LDL-R at the earliest time point, regardless of expression of ChaC1, indicating that glutathione depletion also had no drastic effect on the earlier oxidative phase of LDL-R maturation (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by non-reducing SDS-PAGE data showing similar LDL-R mobility.

claim: LDL-R maturation is unaffected by global depletion of cellular glutathione effected by combined expression of ER-ChaC1CtoS and exposure to buthionine sulfoxide (BSO).
source: LDL-R maturation was also unaffected by further global depletion of cellular glutathione, effected by the combined expression of ER-ChaC1CtoS and exposure to buthionine sulfoxide (BSO), which depleted glutathione globally (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: Supported by pulse-chase data with BSO treatment shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: Expression of active ChaC1 in the ER has no effect on the kinetics of disulfide re-formation on ER-localized roGFP2 following a reductive DTT pulse in cells deficient in ERO1 and PRDX4.
source: Expression of active ChaC1 in their ER had no effect on the kinetics of disulfide re-formation on ER-localized roGFP2 following a reductive DTT pulse (Figure 4F–G), further attesting to the dispensability of glutathione to thiol oxidation in the mammalian ER.
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging data in oxidase-deficient cells shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: Glutathione is dispensable to thiol oxidation in the mammalian ER.
source: Expression of active ChaC1 in their ER had no effect on the kinetics of disulfide re-formation on ER-localized roGFP2 following a reductive DTT pulse (Figure 4F–G), further attesting to the dispensability of glutathione to thiol oxidation in the mammalian ER.
evidence: Inferred from lack of effect of glutathione depletion on roGFP2 oxidation kinetics.

claim: The degradation of misfolded NHK-A1AT requires the action of the reduced form of ERdj5.
source: The degradation of misfolded NHK-A1AT requires the action of the reduced form of a specialized PDI, ERdj5 (Ushioda et al., 2008; Hagiwara et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on NHK-A1AT degradation.

claim: The stability of NHK-A1AT is unaffected by active ER-ChaC1CtoS in both HeLa cells and 293T cells.
source: The stability of NHK-A1AT was unaffected by ChaC1 both in HeLa cells (Figure 5A,D) and in 293T cells (Figure 5B,E).
evidence: Supported by pulse-chase data in two different cell types shown in Figure 5A-E.

claim: Depletion of total cellular pools of glutathione by coincidental exposure to BSO has no effect on NHK-A1AT half-life.
source: Furthermore, depletion of total cellular pools of glutathione by coincidental exposure to BSO had no effect on NHK-A1AT half-life (Figure 5C,F), complementing the evidence for the dispensability of glutathione for ER-associated degradation of this redox-dependent substrate.
evidence: Supported by pulse-chase data with BSO treatment shown in Figure 5C,F.

claim: Glutathione is dispensable for ER-associated degradation of NHK-A1AT.
source: Furthermore, depletion of total cellular pools of glutathione by coincidental exposure to BSO had no effect on NHK-A1AT half-life (Figure 5C,F), complementing the evidence for the dispensability of glutathione for ER-associated degradation of this redox-dependent substrate.
evidence: Inferred from lack of effect of glutathione depletion on NHK-A1AT degradation.

claim: Thiol redox reactions contribute to protein folding homeostasis in the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Thiol redox reactions contribute to protein folding homeostasis in the endoplasmic reticulum. This is reflected in enhanced signaling in the endoplasmic reticulum unfolded protein response (UPR) in cells impaired in ER thiol redox (Frand and Kaiser, 1998; Pollard et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies showing UPR activation in redox-impaired cells.

claim: Enhanced signaling in the UPR occurs in cells impaired in ER thiol redox.
source: Thiol redox reactions contribute to protein folding homeostasis in the endoplasmic reticulum. This is reflected in enhanced signaling in the endoplasmic reticulum unfolded protein response (UPR) in cells impaired in ER thiol redox (Frand and Kaiser, 1998; Pollard et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Neither active nor inactive ER-ChaC1CtoS-mCherry-KDEL measurably affects the basal activity of the CHOP::GFP UPR reporter.
source: Dual-channel FACS analysis revealed that neither active nor inactive ER-ChaC1CtoS-mCherry-KDEL measurably affected the basal activity of a stably integrated mammalian UPR reporter, CHOP::GFP (Novoa et al., 2001) (reflected in the absence of a shift to the right in the mCherry positive population of cells, Figure 6A, left column).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The activity of the CHOP::GFP reporter increased by tunicamycin is unaffected by ChaC1.
source: Furthermore, the activity of the CHOP::GFP reporter, which was increased by tunicamycin, a toxin that perturbs protein folding homeostasis in the ER, was unaffected by ChaC1 (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data with tunicamycin treatment shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The indifference of the UPR to ER-ChaC1CtoS suggests that the dispensability of glutathione observed for LDL-R and NHK-A1AT likely extends to the bulk of proteins that fold oxidatively in the ER under normal cell culture conditions.
source: The indifference of the UPR to ER-ChaC1CtoS is observed over a broad range of unfolded protein stress and over a broad range of ER-ChaC1CtoS-mCherry-KDEL expression, and suggests that the lesson learned from the sentinel proteins, LDL-R and NHK-A1AT likely extend to the bulk of proteins that fold oxidatively in the ER under normal cell culture conditions.
evidence: Inferred from lack of UPR activation across multiple conditions of ER stress and ChaC1 expression.

claim: A hyperactive mutant of ERO1 (C104A, C133A; ERO1*) modestly activates the UPR.
source: Introduction of the C104A; C133A human ERO1L (ERO1*), expressed from a plasmid tagged with the CD2 surface marker indeed modestly activated the UPR, whether measured in cells stably expressing the CHOP::GFP transcriptional reporter (Figure 6B, reflected in the higher GFP levels of cells co-expressing the CD2 marker which tags the ERO1*-expressing cells, panels 2, 4, and 7) or an XBP1::Venus splicing reporter (Iwawaki et al., 2004) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data showing increased UPR reporter activity in ERO1*-expressing cells.

claim: Co-expression of active ChaC1CtoS has no evident synergistic effect with ERO1* on UPR activity beyond that observed with the enzymatically inactive E116Q mutant enzyme.
source: However, co-expression of active ChaC1CtoS had no evident synergistic effect with ERO1* on UPR activity beyond that observed with the enzymatically inactive E116Q mutant enzyme.
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis comparing UPR activity in cells co-expressing ERO1* with active vs inactive ChaC1.

claim: Glutathione is dispensable for the function of the ER even under hyperoxidizing conditions.
source: These findings indicate that glutathione is dispensable for the function of the ER even under hyperoxidizing conditions.
evidence: Inferred from lack of synergistic effect between ERO1* and ChaC1 on UPR activity.

claim: Disulfide bonds have a critical role in stabilizing correctly folded secreted and membrane proteins.
source: Disulfide bonds have a critical role in stabilizing correctly folded secreted and membrane proteins (Fass, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous review.

claim: Dedicated enzymatic machinery consisting of disulfide exchange catalysts of the protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) class rapidly introduces disulfide bonds into nascent polypeptide chains.
source: Dedicated enzymatic machinery, consisting of disulfide exchange catalysts of the protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) class, rapidly introduces disulfide bonds into nascent polypeptide chains.
evidence: Represents established knowledge about ER protein folding machinery.

claim: The recycling of PDIs back to their oxidized form is mediated by upstream oxidases, exemplified by ERO1 and back-up enzymes, such as PRDX4 and VKOR.
source: The recycling of PDIs back to their oxidized form is mediated by upstream oxidases, exemplified by ERO1 and back-up enzymes, such as PRDX4 and VKOR that exploit O2, H2O2, and vitamin K epoxide, respectively, as downstream electron acceptors.
evidence: Represents established knowledge about ER oxidative machinery.

claim: ERO1, PRDX4, and VKOR exploit O2, H2O2, and vitamin K epoxide, respectively, as downstream electron acceptors.
source: The recycling of PDIs back to their oxidized form is mediated by upstream oxidases, exemplified by ERO1 and back-up enzymes, such as PRDX4 and VKOR that exploit O2, H2O2, and vitamin K epoxide, respectively, as downstream electron acceptors.
evidence: Represents established knowledge about electron acceptors for ER oxidases.

claim: Defects in components of the electron transfer chain markedly affect protein folding homeostasis in the ER.
source: Defects in components of this electron transfer chain markedly affect protein folding homeostasis in the ER (Sevier and Kaiser, 2008; Rutkevich and Williams, 2012; Zito, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Many disulfides introduced by the oxidative machinery are not native and must be broken down in an editing process that is catalyzed by reduced forms of PDIs.
source: Many disulfides introduced by the oxidative machinery are not native and must be broken down in an editing process that is catalyzed by reduced forms of PDIs (Hatahet and Ruddock, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous review.

claim: Disulfide editing entails attack by the reduced N-terminal cysteine of PDI's active site on the misplaced disulfide following resolution of the mixed disulfide.
source: This editing entails attack by the reduced N-terminal cysteine of PDI's active site on the misplaced disulfide following resolution of the mixed disulfide.
evidence: Represents established mechanistic knowledge about PDI function.

claim: Both disulfide editing mechanisms require a pool of reduced PDI.
source: Both mechanisms require a pool of reduced PDI, the maintenance of which is not trivial, given the oxidative environment in the ER.
evidence: Represents established knowledge about PDI redox requirements.

claim: PDI's ability to accelerate folding is optimal in a redox buffer that contains a high concentration of reduced glutathione.
source: The crucial role of reduced PDI to oxidative protein folding is supported by in vitro experiments in which PDI's ability to accelerate folding is not monotonically increased by its oxidized fraction, but rather is optimal in a redox buffer that also contains a high concentration of reduced glutathione (Lyles and Gilbert, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous in vitro study.

claim: Disulfide shuffling (which requires reduced PDI) is PDI1's essential function in yeast.
source: Yeast genetics reveal that disulfide shuffling (which requires reduced PDI) is PDI1's essential function, as an active-site mutant that has lost the ability to produce disulfides (but has selectively retained activity as a disulfide reductase) is nonetheless able to rescue the lethal phenotype of pdi1 nullizygosity (Laboissiere et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous yeast genetics study.

claim: Most disulfides that form early during LDL-R biogenesis are non-native and must be rearranged before the protein clears ER quality control and traffics to the Golgi.
source: The reductive facet of oxidative protein folding in the ER is especially important to the maturation of large proteins such as the low density lipoprotein receptor (LDL-R), in which it has been estimated that most disulfides that form early during biogenesis are non-native and must be rearranged before the protein clears ER quality control and traffics to the Golgi (Jansens et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on LDL-R maturation.

claim: The LDL-R editing process appears to involve a specific PDI family member, ERdj5.
source: This editing process appears to involve a specific PDI family member, ERdj5 (Oka et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: ERdj5 may have specialized in disulfide reduction, as its redox function accelerates the clearance of misfolded ER proteins such as NHK-A1AT.
source: ERdj5 may have specialized in disulfide reduction, as its redox function also accelerates the clearance of misfolded ER proteins such as the null Hong Kong mutant α1-antitrypsin (NHK-A1AT) (Ushioda et al., 2008; Hagiwara et al., 2011), but the identity of ERdj5's reductase remains unknown.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies, with speculation about ERdj5 specialization.

claim: The identity of ERdj5's reductase remains unknown.
source: ERdj5 may have specialized in disulfide reduction, as its redox function also accelerates the clearance of misfolded ER proteins such as the null Hong Kong mutant α1-antitrypsin (NHK-A1AT) (Ushioda et al., 2008; Hagiwara et al., 2011), but the identity of ERdj5's reductase remains unknown.
evidence: Explicit statement of knowledge gap.

claim: In E. coli periplasm, the transfer of electrons from reduced thioredoxin in the cytosol maintains a reduced pool of the periplasmic isomerases, DsbC and DsbG.
source: Reductive editing of disulfides is also observed in the E. coli periplasm. Where the transfer of electrons from reduced thioredoxin in the cytosol maintains a reduced pool of the periplasmic isomerases, DsbC and DsbG.
evidence: Represents established knowledge about bacterial disulfide reduction system.

claim: Electrons are conveyed across the inner-membrane space in E. coli by a specialized transmembrane protein DsbD.
source: Electrons are conveyed across the inner-membrane space by a specialized transmembrane protein DsbD.
evidence: Represents established knowledge about bacterial electron transfer.

claim: The protein relay-based mechanism in E. coli enables DsbC/DsbG-dependent disulfide shuffling despite the absence of a soluble small molecule redox buffer in the periplasmic space.
source: This protein relay-based mechanism enables DsbC/DsbG-dependent disulfide shuffling despite the absence of a soluble small molecule redox buffer in the periplasmic space of gram negative bacteria (reviewed in Cho and Collet, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to review article.

claim: The mammalian ER contains up to 15 mM glutathione.
source: By contrast, the mammalian ER contains up to 15 mM glutathione (Montero et al., 2013) whose reduced form is widely believed to fuel the reductive aspects of secreted protein metabolism in eukaryotes, by serving as a terminal electron donor to reduce PDI family members (reviewed in Kojer and Riemer, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Reduced glutathione is widely believed to fuel the reductive aspects of secreted protein metabolism in eukaryotes by serving as a terminal electron donor to reduce PDI family members.
source: By contrast, the mammalian ER contains up to 15 mM glutathione (Montero et al., 2013) whose reduced form is widely believed to fuel the reductive aspects of secreted protein metabolism in eukaryotes, by serving as a terminal electron donor to reduce PDI family members (reviewed in Kojer and Riemer, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to review article describing prevailing belief.

claim: In yeast, deletion of GSH1 does not adversely affect the maturation of the disulfide-bonded lysosomal hydrolyze CPY.
source: The dispensability of glutathione to reductive processes in the ER has been hinted at previously: in yeast deletion of GSH1 (encoding gamma glutamylcysteine synthetase that performs the rate-limiting step in glutathione biosynthesis) does not adversely affect the maturation of the disulfide-bonded lysosomal hydrolyze CPY (Frand and Kaiser, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous yeast study.

claim: The extent of ER glutathione depletion attained by GSH1 deletion in yeast is unclear.
source: However, the extent of ER glutathione depletion attained by this genetic manipulation is unclear and, given the essential role of cellular glutathione to yeast growth, may have been limited by toxicity.
evidence: Speculation about limitations of previous yeast study.

claim: The abolition of the kinetic advantage of Grx1-roGFP2 over roGFP2 in cells expressing enzymatically active ChaC1 argues that glutathione levels were purged to micromolar levels.
source: In vitro the re-oxidation of Grx1-roGFP2 is half-maximal at 18 µM glutathione (Figure 3D). Thus, the abolition of the kinetic advantage of Grx1-roGFP2 over roGFP2 in cells expressing enzymatically active ChaC1 argues that, despite the enzyme's relative low affinity for its substrate (in the millimolar range, Kumar et al., 2012; and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D), glutathione levels were purged to micromolar levels by the high concentration of the enzyme.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of in vitro Kmax0.5 and in vivo probe behavior.

claim: Transport of glutathione into the ER from its site of synthesis in the cytosol is slow.
source: Thus, the preservation of total cellular glutathione levels in cells expressing high levels of ChaC1 in their ER confirms that transport of glutathione into the ER, from its site of synthesis in the cytosol, is slow (as suggested by Kumar et al., 2011), and therefore, that depletion of ER stores by ChaC1 is profound.
evidence: Inferred from differential effects on total cellular glutathione, with supporting citation.

claim: Depletion of ER glutathione stores by ChaC1 is profound.
source: Thus, the preservation of total cellular glutathione levels in cells expressing high levels of ChaC1 in their ER confirms that transport of glutathione into the ER, from its site of synthesis in the cytosol, is slow (as suggested by Kumar et al., 2011), and therefore, that depletion of ER stores by ChaC1 is profound.
evidence: Inferred from preservation of total cellular glutathione despite ER-localized ChaC1 activity.

claim: The redundancy of glutathione could be explained by other small molecule thiols fueling reduction in the ER.
source: The redundancy of glutathione could be explained by other small molecule thiols fueling reduction in the ER. These may even include cysteinyl-glycine, one of the glutathione breakdown product of ChaC1 action.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed glutathione dispensability.

claim: Eukaryotes may have a protein-driven apparatus akin to bacterial DsbD for ferrying reducing equivalents from the cytosol to reduce PDI family members.
source: Alternatively, eukaryotes may have a protein-driven apparatus akin to bacterial DsbD for ferrying reducing equivalents from the cytosol to reduce PDI family members.
evidence: Speculative alternative explanation for glutathione dispensability.

claim: ER glutathione equilibrates with protein thiols.
source: Despite its apparent dispensability, ER glutathione does equilibrate with protein thiols (Appenzeller-Herzog et al., 2010), indicating that it is a redox buffer in the organelle.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: ER glutathione is a redox buffer in the organelle.
source: Despite its apparent dispensability, ER glutathione does equilibrate with protein thiols (Appenzeller-Herzog et al., 2010), indicating that it is a redox buffer in the organelle.
evidence: Inferred from equilibration with protein thiols.

claim: It is possible that despite seemingly rapid equilibration of glutathione to protein thiol redox, the kinetics are insufficient to render glutathione essential.
source: However, it is possible that despite seemingly rapid equilibration of glutathione to protein thiol redox, the kinetics are insufficient to render glutathione essential and that other, even faster processes, maintain an adequate pool of reduced and oxidized PDIs in the mammalian ER, with glutathione following passively.
evidence: Speculative explanation reconciling glutathione equilibration with its dispensability.

claim: ERO1-deficient cells with compromised ER thiol oxidative power have an elevated ratio of oxidized to reduced glutathione.
source: It is noteworthy, in this vein, that ERO1-deficient cells, with compromised ER thiol oxidative power, have an elevated ratio of oxidized to reduced glutathione (Appenzeller-Herzog et al., 2010; Rutkevich and Williams, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Depletion of glutathione by GSH1 deletion rescues the oxidative defect in ERO1-deficient yeast.
source: Across distant phyla, ER redox is not indifferent to cellular glutathione levels. Depletion of glutathione, by GSH1 deletion, rescues the oxidative defect in ERO1-deficient yeast (Cuozzo and Kaiser, 1999), and cytosolic glutathione influences disulfide-bonding of glutenin in the ER of wheat endosperm (Lombardi et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous yeast study.

claim: Cytosolic glutathione influences disulfide-bonding of glutenin in the ER of wheat endosperm.
source: Across distant phyla, ER redox is not indifferent to cellular glutathione levels. Depletion of glutathione, by GSH1 deletion, rescues the oxidative defect in ERO1-deficient yeast (Cuozzo and Kaiser, 1999), and cytosolic glutathione influences disulfide-bonding of glutenin in the ER of wheat endosperm (Lombardi et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous plant study.

claim: Prolonged (48 hr) depletion of glutathione by high concentrations of BSO (1 mM) synergizes with ER hyperoxidation to degrade cell viability.
source: Prolonged (48 hr) depletion of glutathione by high concentrations of BSO (1 mM) synergize with ER hyperoxidation to degrade cell viability (Hansen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Glutathione overload in yeast cells over-expressing HGT1 compromises protein folding in the ER and triggers an unfolded protein response.
source: Glutathione over-load in these cells compromises protein folding in the ER and triggers an unfolded protein response, the basis of which appears to be unregulated re-cycling of PDI from its oxidized to its reduced state imposed by the excessive glutathione (Kumar et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous yeast study.

claim: Over-expression of wild-type cytosolic ChaC1 in mouse ganglionic eminence cells profoundly inhibits the maturation of the Notch precursor to its furin-cleaved form.
source: In mammalian cells too, glutathione stands to impact the maturation of some secreted or membrane proteins: In a study agnostic of its enzymatic activity, over-expression of wild-type cytosolic ChaC1 in mouse ganglionic eminence cells profoundly inhibited the maturation of the Notch precursor to its furin-cleaved form (Chi et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Anti-oxidants that restore impaired glutathione metabolism to normality improve the capacity of liver cells to secrete factor VIII.

claim: ER glutathione is not generally required to maintain protein thiol redox nor folding homeostasis in the ER of cultured mammalian cells.
source: Thus, conservatively interpreted, our observations lead to the conclusion that ER glutathione is not generally required to maintain protein thiol redox nor folding homeostasis in the ER of cultured mammalian cells.

claim: The mammalian pro-apoptotic gene ChaC1 encodes a glutathione-specific γ-glutamyl cyclotransferase that efficiently degrades glutathione.
source: Kumar et al. recently reported that the mammalian pro-apoptotic gene ChaC1 encodes a glutathione-specific γ-glutamyl cyclotransferase that efficiently degrades glutathione (Kumar et al., 2012).

claim: ChaC1 has a relative low affinity for its substrate in the millimolar range.
source: Thus, the abolition of the kinetic advantage of Grx1-roGFP2 over roGFP2 in cells expressing enzymatically active ChaC1 argues that, despite the enzyme's relative low affinity for its substrate (in the millimolar range, Kumar et al., 2012; and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D), glutathione levels were purged to micromolar levels by the high concentration of the enzyme.
evidence: Supported by citation and reference to supplemental figure data.
